text:
Fieldwatch

I built Fieldwatch as a personal tool to see which Wi-Fi access points and Bluetooth LE devices my phone could detect, so I could better understand what was operating around me. It is entirely passive and only listens. There is no dongle, no account, and no backend server. It works offline in the field.

My goals were a modern, easy-to-use interface; flexible, customizable views; a filtering engine so I only see what matters; an extensible signature library so I can identify as many radio sources as possible and add new ones on the fly; and the ability to generate reports of what was observed.

I have been using it and iterating on it for a while now, and it has been useful enough that I thought I would share it.

This is a hobby — something I do for fun in my spare time. There is no Fieldwatch backend. There are no ads. Everything lives on the phone. Source and sideload files are in this repository ( dist/ for the APK, instruction card, and manual).

If you spot an error, something stupid, or have a feature idea — in the app or the documentation — please open an issue on this repository. This is how we make it better. I hope you find it as useful as I have. I look forward to hearing how it goes.

 Just want to install it? Download Fieldwatch.apk. Instruction card and manual: instruction.txt, Fieldwatch User Manual.pdf. What’s new is the changelog for each build. Leave the APK named Fieldwatch.apk . GitHub may say the file is too big to preview — that is their viewer; use Download.

There is a lot of functionality in Fieldwatch. I wrote a comprehensive user guide, and I encourage you to download it so you can get the most out of the app.

 Stay updated. Fieldwatch isn't on the Play Store. Once it is installed, opening the app while the phone is online checks GitHub for a newer build. If there is one, Fieldwatch shows the release notes. Update now downloads it. Android still asks you to confirm the install. Later sets that build aside until a newer one is published. Settings has Check for an update if you want to look yourself. Obtainium can still watch 

 Official builds. The only official Fieldwatch builds are the releases in this repo. Other builds and translations are not made or reviewed by Off Grid Pete LLC.

 On the phone

 
 
 
 
 Signatures 
 More than 250 signatures, in classes. Bookmark one to alert, or add your own.
 
 
 
 Bluetooth floods 
 A burst of new pairing addresses at the same loudness. The advertisement does not name the tool.
 
 
 
 GPS 
 A warning when this phone's GPS changes in a way that can mean interference. It does not say where that came from.
 
 
 
 
 
 Trusted networks 
 A Wi-Fi name you marked can warn if it comes back weaker, from a new maker, or far from its usual places.
 
 
 
 Known cameras 
 Saved lists of plate readers and other sensors. Those marks sit on the map with the radios the phone hears.
 
 
 
 Live map 
 What the phone hears, on the path you walked.
 
 
 
 
 
 Hunt 
 Walk a Bluetooth radio down by loudness. Warmer color is where this phone heard it stronger.
 
 
 
 Filters 
 Cut the list to Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, a strong signal, what moves with you, or what is new.
 
 
 
 Reports 
 A sit keeps a debrief, a path, an export, and a compare against another sit.
 
 
 
 
 
 Cell connection 
 A warning when this phone camps on a cell it has not used here. It does not name a cause. The numbers in the shot are an example.
 
 
 
 How it learns 
 Off until you turn it on. The first still visit only learns. A later new cell can warn.
 
 
 
 Tracker monitoring 
 Warns when a tag says it's away from its owner, your phone has heard it for 30 minutes with no gap over 20 minutes, and hears it at three places at least 100m apart.
 
 
 

One phone. Wi-Fi, Bluetooth LE, this phone's GPS, and this phone's cell connection. The map and the sit stay on the device.

 Technical papers

These are the longer write-ups of Fieldwatch, what each one measures, and what a warning is allowed to mean. The signature file has its own repository. The user guide stays the how-to. Each paper stands alone.

- Radio signature interchange. Fieldwatch uses this proposal so apps can share libraries of known radios.
- Scanning Wi-Fi and Bluetooth for known radios. A place full of radios, and a list that still has to be readable.
- Flood monitoring. When the list of radios stops being a list a person can read.
- GNSS monitoring on the phone in your hand. When the position gets worse, and what a phone is allowed to say about it.
- Trusted networks. A familiar name on the Wi-Fi list, and what a scan can say before anyone joins.
- Cell connection monitoring. Bars on the phone, and no record of the cell behind them.

 Safety & disclaimer

This is a hobby project, provided as-is under the MIT License. A few things to know before you do:

- Use at your own risk. Using Fieldwatch is your responsibility. To the maximum extent permitted by law, Off Grid Pete LLC is not liable for indirect, incidental, special, consequential, or punitive damages arising from its use.
- There is no guarantee that trackers, cameras, tags, access points, or any other device will be found, named, or reported. Radios that are off, cellular-only, asleep, randomized, quiet, or outside what this handset’s OS exposes will not appear. Each phone has its own radios, firmware, scan quotas, and OEM battery policies. Software cannot address those limits.
- Pattern matches, GPS co-travel (“Moving with you” / “possible tail”), Debrief language, and AI Export output are hypotheses — not identity, not a legal finding, and not a complete RF capture. You are solely responsible for how you use this app and this document, and for complying with local law. By using the software or this manual you accept these terms and the MIT License.
- Location data, if tagging is on, is this phone at hear-time — not the other radio. There is no Fieldwatch server. Stamps stay on the handset until you share them. Logs keep full coordinates

install.title: Upgrading from 1.0.4 or earlier — Fieldwatch now has a real publisher certificat
install.html:
This release is a little more professional about how the APK is signed. Android attaches a certificate to every app so the phone can tell “this update is from the same publisher as the app I already have.” Through 1.0.4, Fieldwatch used the generic Android developer certificate that the build tools ship with. That is normal while you are iterating, but people who scan a sideload APK (and some scanners) flag it: a public build should not look like a debug leftover. 1.0.5 is signed with an Off Grid Pete LLC certificate instead. Same hobby app; the file now has a publisher name scanners can check. The fingerprint is in instruction.txt if you want to compare.

The catch is one-time. The phone treats a new certificate as a different publisher, so it will not install 1.0.5 on top of 1.0.4 or earlier. You uninstall the old Fieldwatch, then install this APK. After that, later versions use the same certificate, so ordinary updates work again. You will not have to uninstall for 1.1.44.

Uninstall wipes what is on the phone. If you added signatures, changed Settings, named radios, or saved filter presets, do this first: Settings → Export signatures and Export settings. Share or save those two files somewhere you can get them after. They are not the log and not GPS. Then uninstall (long-press the Fieldwatch icon, or adb uninstall app.fieldwatch), install 1.0.5, open it, tap through the disclaimer, and use Import signatures and Import settings. If you never customized, skip the export and just uninstall, then install.
